planting.note: Set divisions or dormant rhizome pieces in fall into moist, humus-rich conifer-forest soil in deep to dappled shade, mimicking the duff layer where it naturally colonizes among moss.

directions: Oregon anemone is a low spring ephemeral of moist Douglas-fir and western hemlock forests from British Columbia to northern California, producing a single blue, purple, or white flower above three-lobed leaflets before going dormant by midsummer. It spreads slowly by shallow rhizomes through mossy duff and resents disturbance, so established clumps should be left undivided for several years once sited. Give it the same cool, consistently moist, acidic woodland soil it would find under a closed conifer canopy, and avoid summer irrigation extremes that differ from its natural wet-winter, dry-shade-under-canopy cycle. It combines well with trillium and fairybells in a shaded native border where its early bloom precedes the closing forest canopy.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in fall into cool, deeply shaded, humus-rich soil along a streambank-like slope that stays moist through winter and spring.

directions: Endemic to the moist Coast Range and western Cascade forests of Oregon, this obscure trillium relative produces a pair of mottled, strap-shaped leaves each winter followed by small yellow-and-purple flowers that give off a faint carrion odor to attract fungus-gnat pollinators in late winter. It is a true cool-season ephemeral, dying back by early summer once the forest canopy closes overhead, and it needs permanently moist, cool, acidic duff rather than garden-standard amended beds. Site it on a shaded slope or streambank where water drains but never fully dries, and leave the leaf litter in place to replicate the undisturbed forest floor it depends on. It is slow to bulk up and best treated as a specimen curiosity for a dedicated native woodland collection rather than mass planting.

planting.note: Transplant divisions or container stock in spring into moist, shaded forest-edge soil; the square mint-family stems root readily where they touch damp ground.

directions: Coast hedge-nettle grows in damp thickets, stream edges, and forest margins from coastal Alaska south through the Cascades and Coast Range into California, forming loose, sprawling clumps of square-stemmed foliage topped by reddish-pink tubular flowers in whorled clusters through summer. It tolerates more filtered light than deep-forest species, making it useful at the sunnier edge of a shaded native planting where soil stays reliably moist. Cut stems back after bloom to keep the lax habit tidy, and expect it to self-sow modestly or spread by rooting at lower nodes in consistently damp ground. Pair it with salmonberry or red osier dogwood at a woodland-edge seep where it will fill gaps between larger shrubs.

planting.note: Tuck rooted mat fragments into crevices of rock gardens, ledges, or well-drained banks in spring; it needs sharp drainage far more than rich soil.

directions: This widespread spikemoss colonizes rocky outcrops, cliff ledges, and thin soil pockets from British Columbia to California, curling its scale-like branches tightly in summer drought and unfurling bright green again with fall rain. Unlike the moister-forest spikemosses, it tolerates considerable sun and dryness once established, making it a good choice for a rock garden or green roof edge within a broader native planting scheme. Press small rooted fragments directly against gritty, fast-draining soil or rock crevices rather than burying them, since it spreads laterally across a surface rather than rooting deeply. Avoid rich, consistently wet soil, which rots the shallow root system faster than drought ever will.

planting.note: Lay rooted stem sections flat over moist, shaded rock, rotten wood, or soil in spring so trailing stems can anchor along their length as they would over streamside boulders.

directions: In contrast to drier-site spikemosses, Douglas' spikemoss is a shade-and-moisture specialist of low-elevation forests in western Washington and Oregon, trailing its flattened, fern-like branches over streamside rocks, mossy logs, and shaded banks that stay wet most of the year. It needs permanently damp, cool conditions and will not tolerate the summer drying that Wallace's spikemoss shrugs off, so site it near a shaded seep, stream edge, or regularly irrigated woodland bed. Let trailing stems drape over rock or rotting wood rather than mounding soil over them, since new roots form along the stem wherever it touches a damp surface. It is a slow, textural groundcover best used at small scale among ferns and other deep-shade natives rather than as a fast-covering mat.

planting.note: Set divisions of the mat in spring into gritty, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in a cool rock garden pocket or open shaded conifer-forest edge.

directions: Partridgefoot forms dense, woody-based evergreen mats of finely divided, fan-shaped leaflets topped by short spikes of small white flowers in early summer, native to subalpine meadows and open conifer forest at mid-to-high elevations from Alaska to the Cascades. At lower garden elevations it performs best with afternoon shade and soil that mimics the cool, gritty, snowmelt-fed conditions of its native habitat rather than typical lowland heat and drought. Trim lightly after flowering only to tidy spent flower stalks; otherwise it needs no routine pruning and resents being smothered by taller neighbors. It is a long-lived rock garden and native groundcover subject best suited to cooler maritime gardens where summer nights stay mild.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in a woodland edge or rocky meadow setting; it forms a low mat rather than an upright shrub.

directions: Dwarf huckleberry is the smallest of the Pacific Northwest's native huckleberries, forming a low, spreading, deciduous mat studded with tiny urn-shaped pink flowers in late spring and sweet, powdery-blue berries by midsummer. It grows naturally in seasonally moist meadows, bog margins, and open rocky forest from low-elevation coastal sites to subalpine slopes, and performs best in acidic, peaty soil that never fully dries out. Unlike taller huckleberry shrubs it spreads by rhizome into a dense low carpet, making it a useful edible groundcover at the sunnier fringe of a native shade planting. Give it consistent moisture and avoid lime or heavy clay, which quickly cause chlorosis and decline in this acid-loving species.
